questions.text: What is the bearing wall classification threshold per NSCP 2015?

options.text: Greater than 1.45 kN/m superimposed load
Greater than 2.90 kN/m superimposed load
Any vertical load in addition to its own weight
Only loads exceeding the weight of the wall itself

rationale.a: 1.45 kN/m was the legacy NSCP 2010 threshold for light-frame bearing walls.
rationale.b: 2.90 kN/m was the legacy NSCP 2010 threshold for masonry/concrete bearing walls.
rationale.d: The threshold is not a comparison to wall weight, but the presence of any superimposed vertical load.
rationale.correct: The NSCP 2015 simplified the definition of a bearing wall in Section 202 to any wall supporting any vertical load in addition to its own weight, removing the specific kN/m thresholds found in previous editions.
rationale.takeaway: NSCP 2015 removed numeric load thresholds for bearing wall definitions.

questions.text: A cavity wall has an air space of 120 mm. Does this comply with NSCP 2015 limits?

options.text: Yes, any air space larger than 50 mm is acceptable, provided it does not exceed the maximum allowable thickness for structural stability
No, the maximum thickness of the cavity is 115 mm
No, the maximum thickness is 75 mm, which is the standard for ensuring adequate thermal insulation and moisture control
Yes, if the wall is reinforced concrete, as this material can accommodate larger cavity spaces without compromising structural integrity

rationale.a: While it satisfies the 50 mm minimum, it fails the 115 mm maximum.
rationale.c: 75 mm is a common practical width but not the legal maximum.
rationale.d: Cavity wall requirements in Chapter 7 specifically apply to masonry construction.
rationale.correct: Per NSCP 2015 Section 707.1.4.2, the maximum thickness of the cavity (air space) is 115 mm. A design of 120 mm exceeds this limit and would require special structural justification.
rationale.takeaway: NSCP 2015 Cavity Wall Air Space: Maximum 115 mm.

questions.text: A concrete masonry wall supports a 0.5 kN/m superimposed load. How is this wall classified per NSCP 2015?

options.text: Non-bearing because the load is very small
Bearing wall
Curtain wall
Non-structural partition

rationale.a: This is a common error based on legacy codes that had numeric minimums (like 2.90 kN/m). 2015 removes these minimums.
rationale.c: A curtain wall is an exterior non-bearing wall supported by the building frame, not supporting superimposed loads.
rationale.d: A partition wall is interior and typically non-bearing.
rationale.correct: Under NSCP 2015 Section 202, any wall supporting any vertical load in addition to its own weight is a bearing wall. Even a small superimposed load of 0.5 kN/m triggers this classification.
rationale.takeaway: If it carries any extra weight, it's legally a bearing wall.

questions.text: In retaining wall design, what is the difference between a counterfort and a buttress?

options.text: A counterfort is on the outer face; a buttress is on the inner face, which is a common misconception in structural design.
A counterfort is on the inner (soil) face; a buttress is on the outer (exposed) face
Counterforts are for masonry; buttresses are for timber, which is not typically the case in modern construction practices.
Counterforts resist gravity; buttresses resist wind, which oversimplifies their structural roles.

rationale.a: This reverses the correct orientation. Buttresses are visible; counterforts are buried.
rationale.b: This is the standard engineering distinction based on which side of the wall the support rib is placed.
rationale.c: Both are common in reinforced concrete retaining wall systems.
rationale.d: Both are used to resist the lateral earth pressure of the retained soil.
rationale.correct: Counterforts are structural ribs located on the soil side (back) of the wall and are in tension. Buttresses are located on the front (exposed) side and are in compression.
rationale.takeaway: Counterfort = Soil side (Tension); Buttress = Exposed side (Compression).

questions.text: A wood stud wall supports a superimposed load of 2.0 kN/m. Is this wall classified as bearing or non-bearing per NSCP 2015?

options.text: Non-bearing (superimposed load is below numeric code thresholds), which is a common misinterpretation
Bearing (it supports vertical load in addition to its own weight)
Neither—walls are classified only by lateral resistance, which is not accurate for vertical load considerations
Bearing only if the wall is a shear wall, which is a misunderstanding of the classification criteria

rationale.a: Numeric thresholds (like the 1.45 kN/m limit from NSCP 2010) are no longer used in the 2015 definition; any superimposed load triggers bearing status.
rationale.c: Wall classification is primarily determined by vertical load transmission (bearing vs. non-bearing) and lateral load resistance.
rationale.d: A wall can be bearing without being a shear wall. Bearing status refers to gravity loads, while shear status refers to lateral loads.
rationale.correct: Per NSCP 2015 Section 202, a Bearing Wall is defined as any wall that supports any vertical load in addition to its own weight. Since the wall supports a superimposed load of 2.0 kN/m, it is classified as a bearing wall.
rationale.takeaway: NSCP 2015 Definition: Bearing wall = supports any vertical load + own weight.

questions.text: Why are bearing and non-bearing walls designed differently?

options.text: Bearing walls must resist axial compression from gravity loads; non-bearing walls carry only self-weight and lateral loads
Non-bearing walls are not required to resist wind loads, which means they can be constructed with lighter materials and simpler connections
Bearing walls must be thicker than 200 mm by law, especially in high-rise buildings where additional stability is required
Only bearing walls require foundation anchoring, as they transfer significant loads to the foundation, unlike non-bearing walls

rationale.b: All exterior walls, including non-bearing ones, must be designed to resist wind pressure.
rationale.c: Thickness depends on structural calculation and material (e.g., 150 mm for concrete), not a flat 200 mm rule for all types.
rationale.d: All walls must be properly anchored to the building frame or foundation for stability.
rationale.correct: Bearing walls are structural members designed to transmit vertical loads from the roof or upper floors to the foundation. Non-bearing walls are primarily partitions or cladding that must only support their own mass and resist out-of-plane wind or seismic loads.
rationale.takeaway: Bearing walls transmit superimposed gravity loads; non-bearing walls do not.

questions.text: In a seismic zone, a non-bearing curtain wall is attached to a moment-resisting frame. What is the primary structural concern?

options.text: The wall must carry the weight of the floors above, which requires additional structural support
The wall and its anchors must resist out-of-plane wind and seismic forces and accommodate building drift
The wall must be designed as a shear wall, providing lateral stability to the structure
Non-bearing walls are exempt from seismic design, as they do not contribute to the building's structural integrity

rationale.a: By definition, a non-bearing wall does not support the floors above.
rationale.c: Shear walls are part of the lateral force-resisting system; a curtain wall is a non-structural component.
rationale.d: NSCP Chapter 2 (Loads) and Chapter 6 (Wind) explicitly require seismic and wind design for non-structural components like cladding.
rationale.correct: Curtain walls must be designed to 'drift' with the building frame during an earthquake. The anchors must prevent the wall from falling off (out-of-plane forces) while allowing for horizontal movement relative to the floors.
rationale.takeaway: Curtain walls must accommodate inter-story drift and resist lateral pressures.

questions.text: A cavity wall is designed with an air space of 40 mm. Does this comply with NSCP 2015 limits for masonry?

options.text: Yes, 40 mm is the standard required width for most applications, ensuring adequate insulation and moisture control.
No, the minimum air space (cavity thickness) is 50 mm
No, the maximum air space is 25 mm, which is critical for structural stability and thermal performance.
Yes, provided the wall is less than 3 meters high, which allows for some flexibility in design.

rationale.a: 40 mm is below the legal minimum required for moisture control and drainage.
rationale.c: The maximum thickness is actually 115 mm, not 25 mm.
rationale.d: The 50 mm minimum applies regardless of the wall height to ensure proper drainage and air circulation.
rationale.correct: Per NSCP 2015 Section 707.1.4.2, the minimum thickness of the cavity (air space) in a cavity wall shall be 50 mm. A design of 40 mm is insufficient to satisfy this requirement.
rationale.takeaway: NSCP 2015 Cavity Wall Air Space: Minimum 50 mm.

questions.text: A designer provides a wood stud wall that carries a 0.2 kN/m load from a decorative ceiling. Is this wall bearing?

options.text: No, because the load is purely decorative and does not contribute to structural support.
Yes, it supports vertical load in addition to its own weight
No, wood walls must carry at least 1.45 kN/m to be bearing, according to specific building codes.
Only if the wall is taller than 2.4 meters, which is a common misconception about bearing walls.

rationale.a: The nature of the load (decorative vs. structural) does not change the classification; only the presence of load matters.
rationale.c: 1.45 kN/m is the legacy threshold from NSCP 2010 and is no longer part of the 2015 definition.
rationale.d: Height is not a factor in the basic bearing/non-bearing classification.
rationale.correct: NSCP 2015 Section 202 defines a bearing wall by the presence of any superimposed vertical load. Regardless of the load source (decorative or structural), the addition of 0.2 kN/m classifies it as a bearing wall.
rationale.takeaway: Legacy load thresholds (1.45 and 2.90) are frequently tested as 'trap' answers; the 2015 code uses a qualitative trigger.

questions.text: What distinguishes a parapet wall from other wall types?

options.text: A parapet wall is any exterior wall of a building, typically designed to provide additional structural support
A parapet wall is the portion of a wall that extends above the roofline
A parapet wall is always load-bearing, ensuring stability against lateral forces
A parapet wall carries only seismic loads, specifically designed to resist earthquake forces

rationale.a: Exterior walls include the entire building envelope; a parapet is specifically the portion above the roof.
rationale.c: Parapets are typically non-bearing as they do not support floor or roof loads above them.
rationale.d: Parapets must resist both wind and seismic lateral forces.
rationale.correct: A parapet is defined as that part of any wall entirely above the roof line. It is exposed to environmental loads (wind) on both sides and must be designed as a cantilever.
rationale.takeaway: Parapet = portion of wall above the roof line.
